title: How often should mandatory training be refreshed?
description: How often mandatory training must be refreshed: a register of 28 frequencies fixed by law and regulators, and how to set a risk based cycle where none is set.
shortAnswer: Mandatory training should be refreshed at the frequency a law, standard, or regulator sets where one exists, such as annual bloodborne pathogens training under a US Occupational Safety and Health Administration standard. Where no source sets a frequency, which is common, set the cycle on risk: the consequence of error, how often the task is performed, how quickly the rules change, and what assessment and incident data show. Add event triggers so changes prompt retraining between cycles.
keyTakeaways: Only some frameworks set a refresh frequency. This guide's register lists 28 fixed frequencies; annual is the most common, followed by hours per year quotas and three year cycles.
Where a frequency is set, record the exact source and wording. Where it is not, record the risk rationale for the cycle you chose.
Risk factors for a cycle include consequence of error, how often the skill is used, rate of change, and evidence from assessments and incidents.
Event triggers (a changed rule, procedure, system, or an incident) often matter more than the calendar.
Different roles can have different cycles for the same topic. Some regulators publish example intervals by role while stressing they are examples only.

sections.heading: Is there a legal rule for how often training must be refreshed?

blocks.text: There is no general rule. A refresh frequency applies only where a specific law, standard, code, or regulator sets one for a specific group, and many regimes instead require training that is suitable, adequate, or ongoing without naming an interval. Treat any stated frequency as applying only to the population and topic its source covers.

For example, the PIC/S Guide to GMP, which many medicines regulators adopt, asks for continuing training whose practical effectiveness is "periodically assessed", but it does not set an interval ([PE009-16 Part I, clause 2.11](https://www.tga.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-03/pe-009-16-gmp-guide-part-i-basic-requirements-medicinal-products.pdf)). Requirements of this kind tell you that training must continue and must work, and leave the cycle to you.

Other instruments follow the same pattern. The EU Occupational Safety and Health Framework Directive requires training to be adapted to new or changed risks and "repeated periodically if necessary" ([Directive 89/391/EEC, Article 12](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31989L0391)). Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC) guidelines describe it as desirable to enrich the content and frequency of employee education according to risk ([PPC guidelines](https://www.ppc.go.jp/personalinfo/legal/guidelines_tsusoku/)). Neither names an interval.

sections.heading: Where do laws and regulators set a frequency?

blocks.text: Some instruments do name an interval, usually for a defined group and topic. The register below lists every fixed refresh frequency recorded on this site's regulation pages, as at November 2026: 28 provisions across the United States, Portugal, Australia and the United Arab Emirates. Each row links to the regulation page that cites the primary source. It is not a complete register of every law; check the instruments that apply to your organization in each country where you operate.

blocks.text: Three patterns stand out. **Annual** is by far the most common interval, set in 16 of the 28 provisions, mostly for awareness topics such as security, privacy, harassment and exposure to health hazards. **Hours or credits per year** is the model in 6 provisions, mainly professional continuing education (Portugal's 40 hours, the Medical Board's 50 hours, the SAFE Act's 8 hours, DFSA's 15 hours), where the topic is partly left to the individual or employer. **Every three years** appears in 4 provisions where training is long or practical: forklift evaluations, hazmat, process safety and CPR. The remaining two are California's two year harassment cycle and the five year currency of a food safety supervisor certificate.

Read the type of instrument before relying on a row. A statute or regulation is binding on everyone in scope; a control in the Information Security Manual, an ASIC regulatory guide or an accreditation standard binds through the framework that adopts it. For the detail, see [Portugal Labour Code continuous training](/regulations/portugal-labour-code-continuous-training), [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements), [FINRA continuing education](/regulations/finra-continuing-education-requirements) and [ISM awareness training](/regulations/ism-cyber-security-awareness-training).

blocks.title: Examples are not requirements
blocks.text: Regulators sometimes publish example frequencies. Australia's anti money laundering regulator, AUSTRAC, for instance, gives example ongoing training frequencies, such as every 6 to 12 months for AML/CTF compliance officers and senior management and every 12 months for customer facing personnel, and states that "these are examples only, and the frequency you deliver training must be appropriate to your business" ([AUSTRAC](https://www.austrac.gov.au/industry-and-business/obligations-and-guidance/your-amlctf-program/personnel-due-diligence-and-training/amlctf-training)). Treat regulator examples as a reference point for your risk assessment, not as a rule.

sections.heading: How do you set a refresh cycle when no source sets one?

blocks.text: Set the cycle by assessing risk factors for each topic and role, choosing an interval that matches the result, and recording why. The factors below are the ones most often used; weight them to suit your risk framework.

items: **Consequence of error.** How serious is the harm if someone gets this wrong: to people, customers, the organization, or its license?
**Frequency of use.** Skills used daily are practiced at work. Skills used rarely, such as emergency response or unusual transaction reporting, fade and need more frequent practice.
**Rate of change.** How often do the underlying law, policy, procedure, or system change?
**Evidence of performance.** Assessment results, audit findings, errors, complaints, and incidents show whether current knowledge is holding.
**Role exposure.** People who make the relevant decisions need shorter cycles than those who only need awareness.

sections.heading: What does a risk based refresh cycle look like?

blocks.text: A risk based cycle rates each topic and role on the factors above and maps the result to an interval and a method. The example is illustrative only: topics, ratings, and intervals are invented to show the method and are not recommendations for any regime.

blocks.text: Where a topic is also covered by a set frequency, such as annual bloodborne pathogens training under OSHA or annual security awareness under the ISM, the set frequency is a floor. The risk method can shorten it for some roles but not lengthen it.

sections.heading: What are the steps to set and maintain refresh cycles?

blocks.text: Identify set frequencies, assess risk for everything else, add event triggers, then document and review. Each step has an output that becomes part of your training policy or matrix.

items: **List mandatory topics by role.** Use your [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix). Output: topic by role list.
**Find set frequencies.** For each topic, check the instruments that apply and record the exact wording and source. Output: a register of set frequencies with citations.
**Assess risk for the rest.** Rate each topic and role on the risk factors. Output: a risk rating per cell.
**Choose intervals and methods.** Map ratings to intervals and to a method: full course, short refresher, scenario practice, drill, or assessment only. Output: a refresh schedule.

**Define event triggers.** List the changes that require retraining before the next cycle: new or amended law, policy, procedure, or system; an incident or audit finding; a role change. Output: a trigger list with owners.
**Allow assessment first where suitable.** For stable topics, let people take the assessment first and complete the refresher only if they do not meet the standard. Output: a test out rule.
**Document the rationale.** Record the reasons in the [training policy](/guides/how-to-write-a-training-policy). Output: an approved policy section.
**Review with data.** At least annually, compare assessment and incident data against the cycles and adjust. Output: review minutes and changes.

sections.heading: When should training be refreshed outside the normal cycle?

blocks.text: Refresh outside the cycle whenever the knowledge the training teaches has changed or has been shown not to hold. A calendar cycle alone can leave people working to a superseded rule for most of a year.

Some laws are built on triggers rather than intervals. Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act requires safety and health education on hiring and on a change of work content, and special education before workers are assigned to designated dangerous or harmful operations ([Act, Article 59](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347AC0000000057)). The EU Occupational Safety and Health Framework Directive similarly requires training on recruitment, transfer or change of job, and the introduction of new equipment or technology ([Directive 89/391/EEC, Article 12](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31989L0391)). See [Japan Industrial Safety and Health Act training](/regulations/japan-industrial-safety-and-health-act-training) and [EU OSH Framework Directive training](/regulations/eu-osh-framework-directive-training).

Financial regulators take the same view of rule changes. Japan's Financial Services Agency (FSA) expects training to be updated when national risk assessment or Financial Action Task Force (FATF) material changes ([FSA FAQ](https://www.fsa.go.jp/en/news/2026/20260331/02.pdf)). See [how to update training when a regulation changes](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each outcome to the sources it depends on, so a change to a source can identify the people and outcomes that need retraining rather than triggering a full cycle for everyone. Set frequencies and risk rationale can be recorded against the obligation they come from. The [knowledge governance](/platform/knowledge-governance) page describes this.

faqs.q: Is annual compliance training a legal requirement?
faqs.a: Only where a specific instrument says so for a specific group, such as annual bloodborne pathogens training under 29 CFR 1910.1030 in the United States, the annual Regulatory Element under FINRA Rule 1240, or annual cyber security awareness under ISM-0252 of the Information Security Manual. Portugal's Labour Code sets a minimum number of training hours per year rather than a cycle for any topic. Many other regimes require suitable or ongoing training without a set interval.

faqs.q: Can staff skip refresher training if they pass an assessment?
faqs.a: Where no source prescribes the training itself, a test out approach is often defensible: people who meet the standard on a well designed assessment have shown the knowledge is current. Where a source requires the training to be undertaken at a frequency, check whether an assessment alone would satisfy that wording.

faqs.q: Should every role have the same refresh cycle for a topic?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Roles that make the relevant decisions often need shorter cycles and deeper practice than roles that only need awareness. AUSTRAC's examples, for instance, suggest different intervals for compliance officers, customer facing staff, and other personnel, while stressing they are examples only.

faqs.q: How do we evidence the rationale for our refresh cycles?
faqs.a: Record, for each topic and role, any set frequency with its citation, or the risk ratings and the reasoning for the interval chosen. Keep this in the training policy or matrix, approve it through governance, and record each review. Auditors look for a considered, current rationale rather than a particular interval.
